1.solution:
The number of molecules follows the number of moles.

(A) \(\dfrac{0.4}{2} = 0.2\) mol. (B) \(\dfrac{3.2}{32} = 0.1\) mol. (C) \(\dfrac{16.8}{22.4} = 0.75\) mol. (D) \(\dfrac{11.2}{22.4} = 0.5\) mol.

(C) has the most molecules.

2.subtopic: Position, Electronic Configuration and General Features of d-Block
2.solution: Two 3d elements end in \(4s^1\): chromium, \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^5 4s^1\) (\(Z = 24\)), and copper, \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^1\) (\(Z = 29\)). Half-filled and filled d subshells are extra stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d.

3.subtopic: Ionic and Covalent Bonding, Lewis Structures and Octet Rule
3.solution: A (calcium) loses two electrons to form \(\mathrm{A^{2+}}\); B (chlorine) gains one to form \(\mathrm{B^-}\). Charge balance needs two B for each A: \(\mathrm{AB_2}\) (\(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\)).

4.subtopic: Subatomic Particles, Isotopes, Isobars and Isoelectronic Species
4.solution: Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers. \({}^{40}\mathrm{K}\) and \({}^{40}\mathrm{Ca}\) both have mass number 40. The other pairs are isotopes (same atomic number).

5.subtopic: Electronic Effects, Hybridization, Intermediates and General Reactions
5.solution: In benzyl alcohol, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2OH}\), the OH sits on the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) carbon, which has four single bonds (to the ring carbon, two H and O). It is \(sp^3\) hybridised.

6.subtopic: Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Equation

7.solution: \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = -50000 + 100T\). The reaction is spontaneous when \(\Delta G < 0\), that is \(T < \dfrac{50000}{100} = 500\) K. Of the options only \(450\) K is below 500 K.

8.subtopic: Thermochemistry, Hess's Law and Bond Enthalpy
8.solution: \(\Delta H = \) bonds broken \(-\) bonds formed \(= (436 + 242) - 2(431) = 678 - 862 = -184\) kJ/mol.

9.subtopic: pH, pOH and Ionic Product of Water

10.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium, Ka, Kb and Degree of Dissociation
10.solution: By Ostwald's dilution law \(\alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_b}{c}}\): the degree of dissociation is inversely proportional to the square root of the concentration.

11.subtopic: pH, pOH and Ionic Product of Water
11.solution: A basic solution has \([\mathrm{OH^-}] > [\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\). Equal concentrations mean a neutral solution, excess \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\) an acidic one, and \(\mathrm{pOH} = -\log[\mathrm{OH^-}]\), not \(-\log[\mathrm{H^+}]\).

12.subtopic: Balancing Redox Reactions and Oxidized/Reduced Species
12.solution: In (B) no oxidation number changes: Al stays \(+3\), Cl \(-1\), H \(+1\) and O \(-2\). It is a neutralisation. In (A), (C) and (D) a metal is oxidised and another species reduced.

13.solution: Enantiomers are mirror images that cannot be superimposed on each other, so (C) is false. The others are true: \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) through a planar carbocation gives a racemic mixture, a racemic mixture is optically inactive, and \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) inverts the configuration.

14.subtopic: Electronic Effects, Hybridization, Intermediates and General Reactions
14.solution: The inductive effect is a shift of \(\sigma\)-bond electrons along a chain; the resonance effect is the delocalisation of \(\pi\) electrons (or lone pairs) through conjugated \(\pi\) bonds. (I) and (II) are true.

15.solution: By Hückel's rule a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated system is aromatic when it contains \((4n + 2)\) \(\pi\) electrons, for example 6 in benzene (\(n = 1\)).

16.subtopic: Preparation Methods of Aldehydes and Ketones
16.solution: In the Etard reaction toluene is oxidised by chromyl chloride, \(\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2}\), to a chromium complex that hydrolyses to benzaldehyde.

17.solution: \(\rho = \dfrac{ZM}{a^3N_A}\), so \(Z = \dfrac{\rho\,a^3N_A}{M} = \dfrac{2.7 \times 40}{27} = 4\) (an fcc cell, as for aluminium).

18.subtopic: Types of Solids, Crystal Systems and Properties
18.solution: A: \(8 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = 1\) atom per cell. B: one atom at the body centre. The formula is AB.

19.subtopic: Crystal Defects, Magnetic Properties and Semiconductors
19.solution: An n-type semiconductor needs a group 15 dopant (P, As, Sb) whose fifth electron is free. Boron is in group 13; it creates holes and gives a p-type semiconductor.

21.solution: The lowering of vapour pressure grows with the number of solute particles. Sucrose does not ionise (\(i = 1\)), while NaCl, \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) give 2, 3 and 4 ions. The sucrose solution lowers the vapour pressure least, so its vapour pressure is the highest.

22.subtopic: Types of Solutions, Solubility and Henry's Law
22.solution: Henry's law fails for gases that react chemically with the solvent. \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) forms \(\mathrm{NH_4OH}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) forms \(\mathrm{H_2CO_3}\) in water, so both deviate. \(\mathrm{O_2}\), \(\mathrm{N_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) obey the law.

24.subtopic: Galvanic Cells, EMF, Nernst Equation and Thermodynamics
24.solution:
A cell reaction is spontaneous when \(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{cathode} - E^0_{anode} > 0\), the cathode being where reduction happens.

(A) Ca is oxidised and \(\mathrm{Cd^{2+}}\) reduced: \(-0.403 - (-2.866) = +2.463\) V, spontaneous.

(B) \(-0.136 - 1.08 < 0\); (C) \(-0.257 - 0.799 < 0\); (D) \(-0.763 - 1.68 < 0\): none is spontaneous.

25.subtopic: Molar Conductivity, Kohlrausch's Law and Degree of Dissociation
25.solution: This is Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions: \(\Lambda_m^0 = \nu_+\lambda_+^0 + \nu_-\lambda_-^0\).

26.subtopic: Rate Law, Order, Molecularity and Rate Expression

27.subtopic: First-Order Kinetics, Rate Constant and Half-Life

28.solution: For order n the unit of k is \((\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})^{1-n}\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). It is \(\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}s^{-1}}\), the same as the rate itself, when \(n = 0\).

29.solution: Nanoparticles are nanoscale in all three dimensions, so none of their dimensions is outside the nanoscale: they are zero-dimensional nanostructures.

30.solution: Adsorbed gas molecules lose freedom of movement, so \(\Delta S < 0\). For \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) to be negative, \(\Delta H\) must be negative and large enough to outweigh \(-T\Delta S\). Adsorption is therefore exothermic.

31.subtopic: Colloids, Classification, Coagulation and Hardy-Schulze Rule
31.solution: Lyophilic means solvent loving. These sols form readily on mixing (gum, starch, gelatin) and are reversible. Lyophobic (solvent hating) sols are irreversible and need special methods to prepare.

32.subtopic: Group 16 Chalcogens, Oxygen, Sulphur and Ozone
32.solution: Concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) removes the elements of water from sugar: \(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} \rightarrow 12C + 11H_2O}\). It acts as a dehydrating agent.

33.solution: Perbromate is the strongest oxidising agent of the three and perchlorate the weakest (its reduction is very slow), with periodate between them. Their standard reduction potentials run \(\mathrm{BrO_4^-}\) (about \(1.85\) V) \(> \mathrm{IO_4^-}\) (about \(1.6\) V) \(> \mathrm{ClO_4^-}\) (about \(1.2\) V).

34.subtopic: Inner Transition Elements, Lanthanoids and Actinoids
34.solution: Erbium-doped fibre amplifiers boost signals at about \(1550\) nm, the wavelength used in optical fibre communication.

35.subtopic: Bonding Theories, EAN, Crystal Field, Hybridization and Magnetism
35.solution:
For the same metal and ligand, a higher oxidation state gives a larger crystal field splitting, so \([\mathrm{Co(H_2O)_6}]^{2+} < [\mathrm{Co(H_2O)_6}]^{3+}\): I < II (option A).

Note that I < III is also true: a \(3+\) aqua ion of iron splits more than the \(2+\) aqua ion of cobalt. IV (cyanide, a strong-field ligand) splits far more than II, so (C) is false, and (D) is the reverse of (A).
35.note: two options are true. I < II (Co2+ vs Co3+ aqua, same metal, higher charge) is the intended answer, but I < III is also true (measured: [Co(H2O)6]2+ about 9300 cm^-1, [Fe(H2O)6]3+ about 14000 cm^-1). IV is also printed with the wrong charge (3+ for ferricyanide). Kept PRIVATE.

36.solution: Nitrate, \(\mathrm{NO_3^-}\), carries a negative charge. Ammonia and methylamine are neutral, and hydrazinium, \(\mathrm{N_2H_5^+}\), is positive.

37.solution: The acetate ion replaces bromide: \(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br + CH_3COOAg \rightarrow CH_3COOC_2H_5 + AgBr}\). The product is ethyl acetate.

38.solution:
Acid-catalysed hydration of 1-methylcyclohexene follows Markownikoff's rule. The proton adds to the ring \(\mathrm{CH}\) carbon, giving the more stable tertiary carbocation on the carbon carrying the methyl group; water attacks there.

The product A is 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, structure B.

39.solution: \(\mathrm{RCHO + R'MgX}\) followed by hydrolysis gives \(\mathrm{RCH(OH)R'}\), a secondary alcohol. Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol and ketones give tertiary alcohols.

40.solution: Semicarbazide, \(\mathrm{NH_2NHCONH_2}\), condenses with the carbonyl group to give a semicarbazone, \(\mathrm{R_2C{=}NNHCONH_2}\). Hydroxylamine gives an oxime, hydrazine a hydrazone and phenylhydrazine a phenylhydrazone.

41.solution: Hydrazine condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water: \(\mathrm{R_2C{=}O + H_2NNH_2 \rightarrow R_2C{=}NNH_2 + H_2O}\), a hydrazone.

42.solution: Sodium and ethanol (Mendius reduction) reduce a nitrile to a primary amine: \(\mathrm{RC{\equiv}N + 4[H] \rightarrow RCH_2NH_2}\).

43.subtopic: Chemical Reactions and Basicity of Amines
43.solution: Only primary amines give the carbylamine test (foul-smelling isocyanide with \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\) and alcoholic KOH). Secondary amines can also be acetylated and alkylated, and all amines react in some way with nitrous acid.

44.solution: Silver cyanide is largely covalent, so it attacks through nitrogen: \(\mathrm{RX + AgCN \rightarrow R{-}NC + AgX}\), an isocyanide. (KCN, which is ionic, gives the nitrile.)

45.solution: In the cyclic form of glucose the OH on C-5 adds to the aldehyde group at C-1, closing a six-membered (pyranose) ring as a hemiacetal.

46.solution: Insulin is a compact, water-soluble globular protein. Myosin and keratin are fibrous proteins.

47.solution: Chlorophyll is a porphyrin complex with a \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) ion at its centre.

48.solution: Orlon is polyacrylonitrile, made from acrylonitrile, \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCN}\).

49.solution: Natural rubber (cis-polyisoprene) stretches under force and recovers when released: it is an elastomer.

50.subtopic: Green Chemistry, Principles, Atom Economy and Green Solvents
50.solution: Antipyretics (such as paracetamol) lower body temperature in fever. Analgesics relieve pain and antimicrobials kill microorganisms.

51.subtopic: Modulus and Argument — Polar Form, De Moivre and Square Roots
51.solution:
\(z = \dfrac{1 - i}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{i}{2}\), so \(|z| = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and z lies in the fourth quadrant with argument \(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), that is \(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\).

\(z = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4} + i\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right)\).

52.subtopic: Counting Numbers and Geometric Figures — Digits, Divisibility, Points and Polygons
52.solution:
A cubic \(ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d = 0\) needs \(a \neq 0\): 5 choices. With repetition allowed, b, c and d have 6 choices each.

Total \(= 5 \times 6 \times 6 \times 6 = 1080\).

54.solution:
With \(\cos 5x \neq 0\): \(\cos 3x\sin 5x = \sin 7x\cos 5x\). Doubling and using product formulas: \(\sin 8x + \sin 2x = \sin 12x + \sin 2x\), so \(\sin 12x = \sin 8x\).

Either \(12x = 8x + 2n\pi\), giving \(x = \dfrac{n\pi}{2}\), or \(12x = \pi - 8x + 2n\pi\), giving \(x = \dfrac{(2n + 1)\pi}{20}\).

In \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\): \(x = 0, \dfrac{\pi}{20}, \dfrac{3\pi}{20}, \dfrac{5\pi}{20}, \dfrac{7\pi}{20}, \dfrac{9\pi}{20}\). None makes \(\cos 5x = 0\), so there are \(6\) solutions.

55.subtopic: Forms of a Line, Intersections and Concurrency
55.solution:
The intercepts are \(\dfrac{r}{p}\) and \(\dfrac{r}{q}\), so the area is \(\dfrac{r^2}{2pq} = \dfrac{1}{54}\), giving \(pq = 27r^2 = (3\sqrt{3}\,r)^2\).

So \(3\sqrt{3}\,r\) is the geometric mean of p and q: p, \(3\sqrt{3}\,r\), q are in G.P.

56.subtopic: Angle Between the Pair — Perpendicular Pairs, Lines at a Given Angle and the Bisectors
56.solution:
The line has slope \(-3\). A line of slope m makes \(45^\circ\) with it when \(\left|\dfrac{m + 3}{1 - 3m}\right| = 1\), giving \(m = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) or \(m = 2\).

The lines are \(x + 2y = 0\) and \(2x - y = 0\); their joint equation is \((x + 2y)(2x - y) = 2x^2 + 3xy - 2y^2 = 0\).

57.subtopic: Concentric Circles and Circles Touching a Line or an Axis
57.solution: The point of contact is the foot of the perpendicular from the centre. With \(-1 + 2 + 4 = 5\) and \(1^2 + 2^2 = 5\), the foot is \((-1, 1) - \dfrac{5}{5}(1, 2) = (-2, -1)\).

58.subtopic: Rate of Change and Related Rates

59.solution: \(4a = 48\), so \(a = 12\) and the latus rectum ends are \((\pm 24, 12)\). The triangle with the vertex \((0, 0)\) has base \(48\) and height \(12\): area \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 48 \times 12 = 288\) sq. units.

60.solution: \(\log(2 + x) - \log(2 - x) = \log\left(1 + \dfrac{x}{2}\right) - \log\left(1 - \dfrac{x}{2}\right) \approx \dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{x}{2} = x\) for small x, and \(\tan x \approx x\). The limit is \(1\).

61.subtopic: Logical Equivalence and Algebra of Statements
61.solution:
A: \((\sim q \vee p) \vee (\sim p \vee q)\) contains \(p \vee \sim p\), so it is always true.

B: \(\sim p \vee \sim q \equiv \sim(p \wedge q)\) by De Morgan's law, so the biconditional is always true.

C: \((p \vee q) \wedge \sim p \equiv q \wedge \sim p\), and with \(\wedge \sim q\) it contains \(q \wedge \sim q\): always false.

D: \((p \wedge q) \wedge \sim(p \wedge q)\) is always false.

62.subtopic: Finding Truth Values of Component Statements
62.solution: The implication is false only when \(p \wedge q\) is T and \(r \vee \sim s\) is F. So p and q are T, r is F and \(\sim s\) is F, that is s is T: T, T, F, T.

66.solution: \(R_1 + 3R_2 = (-5 + 6, -3 + 3) = (1, 0)\), so A becomes \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\): every entry above the diagonal is zero, a lower triangular matrix (non-singular, determinant 1).

67.subtopic: Inverse of a Matrix — Adjoint Formula, Products and Verification
67.solution:
\(AA^{-1} = I\), using the first column of \(A^{-1}\):

Row 1: \(2\gamma - \beta = 1\). Row 2: \(5\gamma + \alpha = 0\). Row 3: \(\alpha + 3\beta = 0\).

So \(\alpha = -5\gamma\) and \(\beta = \dfrac{5\gamma}{3}\); then \(2\gamma - \dfrac{5\gamma}{3} = 1\) gives \(\gamma = 3\), \(\alpha = -15\), \(\beta = 5\).

\(|\alpha\beta\gamma| = |-15 \times 5 \times 3| = 225\).

68.solution:
Put \(x^2 = \cos 2\theta\). Then \(\sqrt{1 + x^2} = \sqrt{2}\cos\theta\) and \(\sqrt{1 - x^2} = \sqrt{2}\sin\theta\), and the bracket is \(\dfrac{\cos\theta - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta + \sin\theta} = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \theta\right)\).

So \(y = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(x^2)\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{2x}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}}\).

71.solution:
For small x: \((8 - 2x)^{1/3} = 2\left(1 - \dfrac{x}{4}\right)^{1/3} \approx 2 - \dfrac{x}{6}\), so the numerator is about \(-\dfrac{x}{6}\).

\((243 + 5x)^{1/5} = 3\left(1 + \dfrac{5x}{243}\right)^{1/5} \approx 3 + \dfrac{x}{81}\), so the denominator is about \(-\dfrac{x}{81}\).

\(k = \dfrac{-x/6}{-x/81} = \dfrac{81}{6} = \dfrac{27}{2}\).

72.solution: \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^x}\). Differentiating with respect to y: \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dy^2} = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{1 + e^x}\right)\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{-e^x}{(1 + e^x)^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1 + e^x} = \dfrac{-e^x}{(1 + e^x)^3}\).

74.subtopic: Tangents, Normals, and the Slope of a Curve
74.solution:
\(y = -\dfrac{7}{x}\), so the tangent slope is \(\dfrac{7}{x^2} > 0\) and the normal slope \(-\dfrac{x^2}{7} < 0\).

The slope of \(Ax + By + C = 0\) is \(-\dfrac{A}{B}\); it is negative when A and B have the same sign.

75.solution:
Let x be the square's piece. Area \(= \dfrac{x^2}{16} + \dfrac{(40 - x)^2}{4\pi}\).

Setting the derivative to zero: \(\dfrac{x}{8} = \dfrac{40 - x}{2\pi}\), so \(\pi x = 160 - 4x\) and \(x = \dfrac{160}{\pi + 4}\) (a minimum, since the second derivative is positive). The circle's piece is \(40 - x = \dfrac{40\pi}{\pi + 4}\).

77.solution:
\(\log 225 = 2\log 15\), so the numerator is \(2(15x^{14} + 15^x\log 15) = 2\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{15} + 15^x)\).

The integral is \(2\log(x^{15} + 15^x) + c = \log(x^{15} + 15^x)^2 + c\).

78.subtopic: Trigonometric Integrals - Rational and Substitution Forms
78.solution:
Divide numerator and denominator by \(\cos^4 x\): \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2\tan x\sec^2 x}{1 + \tan^4 x}\,dx\). With \(t = \tan^2 x\), \(dt = 2\tan x\sec^2 x\,dx\): \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dt}{1 + t^2} = \tan^{-1}(\tan^2 x) + c\).

So \(f(x) = \tan^{-1}(\tan^2 x)\) and \(\tan f(x) = \tan^2 x\).

79.solution:
The integrand is \(e^{2x}(\cot 2x - \mathrm{cosec}^2 2x)\).

\(\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^{2x}\cot 2x) = 2e^{2x}\cot 2x - 2e^{2x}\mathrm{cosec}^2 2x = 2e^{2x}(\cot 2x - \mathrm{cosec}^2 2x)\).

So the integral is \(\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}\cot 2x + c\): \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(A^3 = \dfrac{1}{8}\).

81.subtopic: Odd and Even Integrands — Symmetric Limits
81.solution:
The denominator is even, so the odd terms \(2x^9 - 5x^7 + 4x^3 - x\) integrate to zero over symmetric limits.

The even part is \(\dfrac{3x^8 + 9x^6 + 3}{x^2 + 3} = 3x^6 + \dfrac{3}{x^2 + 3}\).

\(2\displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt{3}}3x^6\,dx = \dfrac{6}{7}(\sqrt{3})^7 = \dfrac{162\sqrt{3}}{7}\) and \(2\displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt{3}}\dfrac{3\,dx}{x^2 + 3} = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{2}\).

The value is \(\dfrac{162\sqrt{3}}{7} + \sqrt{3}\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

82.subtopic: Areas of Circles, Ellipses and Hyperbolas — Sectors, Segments and Standard Integrals
82.solution: The curve is the upper half of the ellipse \(x^2 + \dfrac{y^2}{4} = 1\) (\(a = 1\), \(b = 2\)). Its area is half of \(\pi ab = 2\pi\), that is \(\pi\).

84.solution:
Put \(y = vx\): \(v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{1 + v}{1 - v}\), so \(x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{1 + v^2}{1 - v}\).

\(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1 - v}{1 + v^2}\,dv = \int\dfrac{dx}{x}\) gives \(\tan^{-1}v - \dfrac{1}{2}\log(1 + v^2) = \log x + k\), that is \(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{y}{x} = \log\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} + k\).

So \(c(x^2 + y^2)^{1/2} = e^{\tan^{-1}(y/x)}\).

85.solution:
\(\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^2\dfrac{dr}{dt} = k \cdot 4\pi r^2\), so \(\dfrac{dr}{dt} = k\): the radius grows uniformly.

\(r = 2 + kt\) with \(7 = 2 + 5k\), so \(k = 1\) cm/min and at 12 minutes \(r = 14\) cm.

Surface area \(= 4\pi(14)^2 = 784\pi = 784 \times \dfrac{22}{7} = 2464\) sq.cm.

86.solution:
\(\bar{a} \times (\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) = (\bar{a}\cdot\bar{c})\bar{a} - \bar{c}\), so \(\bar{b} = \bar{c} - (\bar{a}\cdot\bar{c})\bar{a}\).

\(|\bar{b}|^2 = |\bar{c}|^2 - 2(\bar{a}\cdot\bar{c})^2 + (\bar{a}\cdot\bar{c})^2 = 4 - (\bar{a}\cdot\bar{c})^2 = 1\), so \((\bar{a}\cdot\bar{c})^2 = 3\).

\(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1 \times 2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) for the acute angle, so \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\).

94.solution:
The line passes through \((2, 3, -2)\) with direction \((-3, 2, 1)\); the vector to \((3, 7, -7)\) is \((1, 4, -5)\).

Normal \(= (-3, 2, 1) \times (1, 4, -5) = (-14, -14, -14)\), that is \((1, 1, 1)\). The plane is \(x + y + z = 3\).

96.solution:
The line \(3x - y = 6\) meets \(y = 0\) at \((2, 0)\) and \(y = 2\) at \(\left(\dfrac{8}{3}, 2\right)\). The region lies to its right, up to \(x = 3\) and between \(y = 0\) and \(y = 2\).

\(g = \dfrac{4\pi^2L}{T^2}\), so \(\dfrac{\Delta g}{g} = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L} + 2\dfrac{\Delta T}{T}\).

\(\dfrac{0.1}{10} = 1\%\) and \(\dfrac{1}{50} = 2\%\). Percentage error \(= 1\% + 2 \times 2\% = 5\%\).

104.subtopic: Dynamics of Circular Motion — Banking, Conical Pendulum, Vertical Circle
104.solution:
For a conical pendulum with the string at angle \(\theta\) to the vertical, the horizontal part of the tension gives the centripetal force: \(T\sin\theta = m\omega^2 L\sin\theta\), so \(T = m\omega^2 L\).

\(\omega = 2\pi \times \dfrac{3}{\pi} = 6\) rad/s, so \(T = 36mL\).

105.solution: The two parts carry equal momenta p. Kinetic energy \(= \dfrac{p^2}{2M}\), so \(\dfrac{K_1}{K_2} = \dfrac{M_2}{M_1}\).

106.subtopic: Rotational Kinetic Energy and Rolling Motion
106.solution: Sliding: \(V = \sqrt{2gh}\). A rolling ring has \(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\left(1 + \dfrac{K^2}{R^2}\right) = mv^2\) (since \(K = R\)), so \(mv^2 = mgh\) and \(v = \sqrt{gh} = \dfrac{V}{\sqrt{2}}\).

107.solution:
Minute hand: \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3600}\) rad/s; hour hand: \(\dfrac{2\pi}{43200}\) rad/s.

Relative speed \(= \dfrac{2\pi(12 - 1)}{43200} = \dfrac{11\pi}{21600}\) rad/s.

108.solution: \(I = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2 = 0.08\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}\), so \(\tau = I\alpha = 0.8\) N m and \(F = \dfrac{\tau}{R} = \dfrac{0.8}{0.4} = 2\) N.

109.subtopic: Gravitational PE, Escape Velocity, and Energy
109.solution:
\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = GMm\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{R + h}\right)\) with \(v^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{2GM}{R}\):

\(\dfrac{1}{4R} = \dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{R + h}\), so \(R + h = \dfrac{4R}{3}\) and \(h = \dfrac{R}{3}\).

111.solution: \(h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}\). With h, T and r the same, \(\cos\theta \propto \rho\), so \(\cos\theta_1 > \cos\theta_2 > \cos\theta_3\) and \(\theta_1 < \theta_2 < \theta_3\).

112.solution: Each droplet has radius \(\dfrac{R}{4}\). New area \(= 64 \times 4\pi\dfrac{R^2}{16} = 16\pi R^2\), an increase of \(12\pi R^2\). Work \(= 12\pi R^2T\).

113.subtopic: Calorimetry, Latent Heat, and Heat Capacity

114.subtopic: Radiation — Stefan, Wien, Newton's Law of Cooling, Black Body
114.solution: Rate \(\propto eT^4\): \(0.2 \times 3^4 = 16.2\), so the rate is \(16.2R\).

115.subtopic: Radiation — Stefan, Wien, Newton's Law of Cooling, Black Body
115.solution: The area becomes \(\dfrac{1}{16}\) of A, and the temperature goes from \(300\) K to \(600\) K, so \(T^4\) grows 16 times. Energy per unit time \(\propto AT^4\) stays \(E\).

116.subtopic: First Law, Internal Energy, and Work-Heat Relations
116.solution: \(\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T\) with \(C_v = \dfrac{R}{\gamma - 1}\) and \(nR\Delta T = P\Delta V = PV\). So \(\Delta U = \dfrac{PV}{\gamma - 1}\).

117.subtopic: Isothermal, Adiabatic, Isobaric, and Isochoric Processes
117.solution: \(v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}\), so T must fall to \(\dfrac{T}{9}\). Adiabatically \(TV^{\gamma - 1} = TV^{0.5}\) is constant, so \(V^{0.5}\) must grow 9 times: the volume grows \(81\) times.

118.solution:
At the extreme \(T_{min} = mg\cos\theta\). At the bottom \(T_{max} = mg + \dfrac{mv^2}{L} = mg(3 - 2\cos\theta)\).

\(3 - 2\cos\theta = 2\cos\theta\) gives \(\cos\theta = 0.75\).

120.subtopic: Progressive Wave, Wave Equation, and Velocity
120.solution: The time between crests is the period, \(T = \dfrac{\lambda}{v} = \dfrac{40}{10} = 4\) s.

121.subtopic: Sound Wave Properties, Speed, and Intensity
121.solution: Wave energy \(\propto n^2A^2\). Equal energies: \(n^2A^2 = \dfrac{n^2}{16}A_Q^2\), so \(A_Q = 4A\).

122.solution: In a stationary wave every particle except the nodes vibrates with the same period, but the amplitude varies with position, from zero at nodes to a maximum at antinodes.

123.solution: In the fundamental mode of a closed pipe \(L = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}\), so the time to travel the pipe is \(t = \dfrac{L}{v} = \dfrac{T}{4}\). The frequency is \(\dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{4t} = \dfrac{0.25}{t}\).

124.solution: The third overtone is the fourth harmonic: 4 loops, which have 5 nodes and 4 antinodes.

125.solution: By symmetry each of the six faces carries \(\dfrac{Q}{6\epsilon_0}\), so two faces carry \(\dfrac{Q}{3\epsilon_0}\).

127.solution: In series the charge is the same, so each potential is inversely proportional to the capacitance. With capacitances KC and C, the air capacitor takes \(V\dfrac{KC}{KC + C} = \dfrac{KV}{K + 1}\).

128.solution: The charge \(C_1V_1\) is shared by the parallel pair of capacitance \(C_1 + C_2\): \(V_2 = \dfrac{C_1V_1}{C_1 + C_2}\).

129.solution: Potential gradient \(= \dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75\) V/m, so 1 m balances \(0.75\) V.

130.solution:
\(\dfrac{R_A}{R_B} = \dfrac{40}{60} = \dfrac{2}{3}\). With \(R = \dfrac{4\rho L}{\pi d^2}\) and equal lengths, \(\rho \propto Rd^2\):

\(\dfrac{\rho_A}{\rho_B} = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 9 = 6\), that is \(6 : 1\).

131.subtopic: Magnetisation, Susceptibility, Permeability, and B-H-M Relations

132.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
132.subtopic: Magnetic Moment of Current Loop and Galvanometer Instruments
132.solution: Inside, \(\Phi = \mu_0\dfrac{N}{l}IA\). The magnetic moment is \(m = NIA = \dfrac{\Phi l}{\mu_0} = \dfrac{\frac{\pi}{2} \times 10^{-6} \times 0.6}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}} = 0.75\ \mathrm{Am^2}\).

133.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
133.subtopic: Magnetic Moment of Current Loop and Galvanometer Instruments
133.solution: Fewer turns means a shorter length of wire in the coil, so the coil's resistance decreases.

134.subtopic: Self-Inductance, Energy Stored, and LR Circuit
134.solution: \(e = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\): the induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a negative sign. Its graph against \(\dfrac{dI}{dt}\) is a straight line through the origin going into negative e, which is graph C.

135.solution: \(e = M\dfrac{dI}{dt} = M\omega I_0\cos\omega t\), whose maximum is \(M\omega I_0\).

136.solution:
The intended working takes the capacitor voltage as \(V = IR\): \(\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}CV^2}{\frac{1}{2}LI^2} = \dfrac{CR^2}{L} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-6} \times 100}{10^{-3}} = 0.2\), option (C).

Physically, maximum current means resonance, where \(X_C = X_L\) and the capacitor's voltage amplitude is \(IX_C\), not IR. Then the peak energies are \(\dfrac{1}{2}C(IX_C)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2\), a ratio of \(1 : 1\), which is not an option.
136.note: at resonance the peak energies in L and C are equal (1:1, not an option). 0.2 (C) is what CR^2/L gives, which treats the capacitor voltage as the applied voltage IR. Kept PRIVATE.

138.subtopic: RMS, Peak, and AC Source Characteristics

140.solution: For a spherical mirror the focus lies midway between the pole and the centre of curvature: \(F = \dfrac{R}{2}\), so \(R = 2F\).

141.solution: \(\tan\theta_B = \mu\), and the refractive index depends on wavelength. So Brewster's angle is different for different colours.

142.subtopic: Young's Double Slit — Fringe Width, Positions and Shifts
142.solution: Angular fringe width \(= \dfrac{\lambda}{d}\), and in water the wavelength is \(\dfrac{\lambda}{\mu}\). So the width becomes \(0.2^\circ \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 0.15^\circ\).

143.solution: Newton's corpuscular theory explained refraction by an attraction of the denser medium, which predicts that light travels faster in glass than in air. So "the velocity of light in air is greater than in glass" is not a property under that theory (it was the wave theory's prediction, later confirmed).

144.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
144.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect — Stopping Potential, Threshold, and Work Function
144.solution: Maximum kinetic energies are \(3W - W = 2W\) and \(5W - W = 4W\). Since \(v \propto \sqrt{K}\), the ratio is \(\sqrt{2} : \sqrt{4} = 1 : \sqrt{2}\).

145.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
145.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect — Stopping Potential, Threshold, and Work Function
145.solution: The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depends on the frequency of the light, not on its intensity. Intensity changes only the number of electrons emitted. So the graph of E against I is a horizontal line: P.

147.solution: The orbiting electron is a current loop with \(M = \dfrac{e}{2m}L\) (the gyromagnetic ratio). So \(L = \dfrac{2mM}{e}\).

148.subtopic: Band Theory, Doping, and Semiconductor Types
148.solution: In a semiconductor more electrons cross the band gap as the temperature rises, so the resistivity falls steeply (roughly exponentially) and then levels off: graph B. Graph D is the rising curve of a metal.

149.subtopic: Transistors — BJT, CE Amplifier, and Gain

150.subtopic: Transistors — BJT, CE Amplifier, and Gain
150.solution: For a transistor amplifier in the usual common emitter mode, the current gain is the change in output (collector) current per change in input (base) current: \(\beta = \dfrac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta I_B}\).
